In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the aromatic and quinoid forms are both important in the electronic properties, and the balance between them can be modulated by the size of the molecule and the oxidation state, as well as the presence of the pro-aromatic quinoxidals.
the aromaticity and quinoidality in these systems are not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary, and that the aromatic and quinoid contributions are in fact synergic.
the aromatic form is the most stable one, but that quinoidals can be more effective in charge transfer, and that the aromatic form can be stabilized by the formation of quinoidal forms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the synergy between the two forms can be tuned by the choice of oligomer length, oxidation states and the presence of electron withdrawing or electron donating groups.
the aromatic form is more important for the oligomeric states and the quinoidal form is more important when redox species are studied.
aromaticity and quinoidality can be considered as two extremes of a continuum of electronic states, which can be tuned by chemical modification of the molecule and/or by external stimuli.
The main takeaway from our work is that

quinoidal vs. aromatic synergy is a general feature of the redox chemistry of conjugated polymers, and it can be tuned by the size and the nature of the polymer backbone, and also by the oxidation state.
quinoidal forms are not necessarily more stable than aromatic ones, but they can be more stable in some cases, while in other cases they are less stable.
